newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia acts to boost private-sector refinery.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia acts to boost private-sector refinery.

text.p: Indonesia, which is increasingly short of refined oil products, has issued new guidelines to make it clearer for the private sector to build refineries and to speed up their development.
Under the guidelines, President Suharto also allowed private refiners to seal joint ventures with state-owned Pertamina.

"In an effort to maintain national development and to strengthen the economy...in refining and processing crude oil and gas, new refineries are needed in order to fulfil domestic needs," Suharto said in a presidential decree dated July 31. A copy of the document was obtained by Reuters on Monday.
"The building of refineries needs big funds, therefore beside increasing the role of the state-owned company, there is a need to encourage private firms to build (the refineries)," Suharto said.
A Pertamina official said the decree would enable the private sector to build refineries with the option of selling oil products to Pertamina.
"The decree gives concrete guidelines to private sector involvement in the refinery businesses," the official told Reuters.
"One new thing in the decree is to allow Pertamina to jointly build refineries with private companies. This is a positive move," he said.
Suharto said in the decree: "Private companies can cooperate with Pertamina in building and operating the refineries through part capital ownership".
The decree said private refineries can be set up by Indonesian companies themselves or in partnership with foreign firms.
It said Pertamina will remain the sole distributor of oil products in the domestic market, but added that products not needed by Pertamina can be exported by private refineries.
The decree said Pertamina will enter into long-term contracts to buy fuel products from private refineries at prices quoted in the international market.
Indonesia has long encouraged the private sector to build new refineries, but without much success because of a lack of proper guidelines.

Industry sources said while Suharto's decree would help to clarify some of the administrative complexities, the main reason why the private sector has been slow in building refineries was their inability to sell directly to the domestic market.
This remains a problem as long as the country's constitution upholds Pertamina as the monopoly in the retail market, which is growing rapidly, they said.
They also said private refiners are not keen to export their products because the region is already very well supplied by refineries in Singapore, South Korea the Middle East and Europe.
The Pertamina official said oil product imports would remain high in the coming years with consumption annual growth of between six and seven percent.
Indonesia now has eight refineries, all operated by Pertamina, with a combined capacity of 989,500 barrels per day (bpd).
The official said Indonesia needs at least two refineries this year with a 125,000-bpd capacity each.
Pertamina has said it imported 11.4 million kilolitres of fuel products in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) and it forecast imports would be around the same level in 1997/98.
